identity_notes: This retrieval was overwhelmingly dominated by content unrelated to phenylalanine SUPPLEMENTATION: (1) phenylketonuria (PKU) disease-management literature (~50 records) covering dietary phenylalanine RESTRICTION and PKU drugs (sapropterin, pegvaliase, sepiapterin) -- the opposite clinical direction from supplementing phenylalanine, rejected off_topic/different_substance throughout; (2) aspartame safety/metabolism literature (~8 records), since aspartame breaks down to phenylalanine but is a distinct artificial sweetener, rejected different_substance; (3) a very large cluster (~30 records) of muscle-protein-synthesis research where phenylalanine is used only as an ISOTOPIC TRACER to measure the effect of some OTHER protein source (whey, collagen, potato, meat, casein, etc.) on synthesis rates -- phenylalanine itself is never the administered intervention in these, rejected not_intervention; and (4) a large cluster of observational metabolomics/biomarker reviews across many diseases (cancer, diabetes, glaucoma, Parkinson's, etc.) where phenylalanine is measured as a biomarker, not administered, rejected not_intervention. After removing these, only 6 genuine oral phenylalanine/D-phenylalanine human trials or reviews remained, and most of their retrieved abstracts were truncated before the results sentence in this scope. The clearest finding is a small crossover trial (3296793) showing D-phenylalanine (20 mg/kg/d) had no effect, positive or negative, on hyperactive-child behavior, though it raised serum phenylalanine -- offered by the original authors as reassurance about aspartame's phenylalanine content rather than as vitiligo/mood evidence. A vitiligo trial (8186511) found L-phenylalanine combined with UVA phototherapy produced repigmentation, but cannot be attributed to phenylalanine alone since it was never tested without UVA in this retrieved scope, and higher phenylalanine doses did not improve response further (ceiling effect).
